newsitem.title: USA: UN mulls Iraq oil contracts as $2 bln limit looms.
newsitem.headline: UN mulls Iraq oil contracts as $2 bln limit looms.

text.p: The United Nations is holding up some Iraqi oil contracts it has in hand over worries that the amount Baghdad has already contracted to sell may exceed the limit set by the "oil-for-food" deal, sources said Friday.

Officially, the U.N. has said that there are 13 contracts approved and none pending. However, sources said that there are a number of contracts which have been "conditionally approved," but are awaiting an assessment of the value of all the contracts Baghdad has signed so far.

"SOMO (Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation) has signed contracts for 525,000 barrels per day on term (contract) and they (the U.N.) are worried that it may have sold too much," said a source close to the U.N. Secretariat, whose overseers must approve the contracts.

Under the terms of the deal Baghdad is allowed to sell up to $2 billion of oil over six months, on a renewable basis, with the proceeds mostly going to pay for badly needed food, medicines and other humanitarian goods for Iraqi civilians.

Since the deal won final approval earlier this month, SOMO has quickly signed deals with around 20 or so oil companies, including contracts with U.S. companies for about 110,000 barrels a day, more than 200,000 bpd with European companies, 75,000 bpd with Turkey's state oil company, 108,000 bpd with Russian concerns and 40,000 bpd with a Japanese trading company.

According to Reuter's estimates, the total contracted for so far is 534,000 bpd, on top of which several other companies are understood to be in negotiations with SOMO, including Texaco Inc of the U.S. and state-owned Petrobras of Brazil.

Contract terms are based on formulas which set the price at a discount to various world benchmark oil prices on the day the oil is due to be shipped, including West Texas Intermediate crude in the U.S.
Oil prices have been erratic lately but recent high oil prices, if they were sustained, would put the value of Iraq's contracts significantly above the $2 billion limit.

"We did look at it and the overseers made a point of saying that it was going to be a difficult issue. If it slips just over the $2 billion then in international law it is illegal," said a diplomat who has been closely involved in the scheme.

German ambassador Tono Eitel, chairman of the U.N. Iraq Sanctions Committee, said after the committee met on Wednesday that the overseers were keeping open the option of scaling back the amount contracted by 10 percent.
Meanwhile, oil companies awaiting approval are concerned that they will lose out on a rare commercial opportunity if the U.N. shuts the door before they get in or if their contracts are scaled back.

"We're taking the first two cargoes into our own system but we will sell it on if we get the right deal. In fact, not the first two but the third cargo we are going to lift we've already sold on," said a source at one of the oil companies awaiting approval.
"I've got six buyers lined up waiting to hear," said a trading company with a pending contract.
-- Tony McAuley, New York Energy Desk, +1 212 859 1623
